title: THE VERSE PAUL USED TO EXPOSE A SECRET ABOUT SEX THAT MANY CHRISTIANS STILL DON'T UNDERSTAND
paragraphs: THE VERSE PAUL USED TO EXPOSE A SECRET ABOUT SEX THAT MANY CHRISTIANS STILL DON'T UNDERSTAND

Why did Paul quote “The two shall become one flesh” while warning against prostitution? The answer reaches all the way back to Eden, exposes what sexual sin does to the human heart, and reveals why the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than even our most shameful past.
“What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh.” — 1 Corinthians 6:16 (KJV)
There is something deeply unsettling about the fact that Paul used a verse about marriage to warn Christians about prostitution.
Think about that.
He could have simply said, “Don't do it. It's a sin.”
He could have reminded the Corinthians of the seventh commandment.
He could have condemned their behavior and moved on.
But he didn't.
Instead, Paul reached backward through centuries of human history, all the way to the Garden of Eden, and pulled out one of the most beautiful declarations God ever made about marriage.
“The two shall become one flesh.”
And then he applied those very words to a man joining himself to a prostitute.
Why?
Why would the apostle take language from the sacred beginning of marriage and place it in the middle of a warning about sexual immorality?
Because Paul wanted the Corinthians to understand something they were dangerously close to forgetting.
Sexual intimacy was never designed to be spiritually insignificant.
And the body was never meant to be treated as though it had nothing to do with belonging to God.
But there is something even more astonishing buried in this passage.
Paul was not merely warning believers about what they could lose through sexual sin.
He was reminding them of Someone to whom they already belonged.
And once you understand that, the entire passage changes.
Because this is not simply a story about prostitution.
It is a story about creation, covenant, human brokenness, redemption, and a Savior who purchased people with His own blood.
And perhaps, before this article ends, you will realize that the question is not merely what you have done with your body.
The deeper question is whether you have truly understood whose you are.
Imagine Corinth.
A prosperous Roman city filled with merchants, travelers, religious traditions, competing philosophies, and countless temptations.
Christianity was spreading through a culture that did not automatically share the moral convictions of the Old Testament Scriptures.
Some believers had come out of backgrounds in which sexual practices were treated very differently from the standards taught by the apostles.
They were learning what it meant to follow Jesus while living in a society that frequently normalized behavior the Gospel called them to abandon.
And apparently, some had begun treating sexual activity as though it were little more than a bodily appetite.
Paul confronted that thinking.
In 1 Corinthians 6:13, he addressed the relationship between the body and the Lord.
Then, in verse 15, he asked a question that should have stopped his readers in their tracks.
“Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?”
Read that again.
Your bodies.
Not merely your thoughts.
Not merely your prayers.
Not merely your Sunday worship.
Your bodies.
Paul was reminding believers that union with Christ was not an abstract religious idea disconnected from their physical lives.
Their bodies belonged to the Lord.
They were members of Christ.
Then came the shocking question:
“Shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid.” — 1 Corinthians 6:15 (KJV)
The force of Paul's argument is extraordinary.
He was not saying that a Christian could somehow turn Jesus into a participant in personal sin.
He was exposing the terrible contradiction of claiming to belong to Christ while deliberately using one's body in a way that dishonors Him.
And then Paul explained why this mattered.
“For two, saith he, shall be one flesh.”
Those words were not invented in Corinth.
They were born in Genesis.
Long before there were cities, temples, brothels, churches, or human systems of religion, God created humanity male and female.
Genesis 2 describes the creation of the woman and the establishment of the marital union.
And in Genesis 2:24, Scripture declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
Literally, “one flesh.”
The Hebrew word basar means flesh, while echad means one.
The phrase communicates the profound unity established between husband and wife.
It includes their bodily union, but the context is larger than a moment of physical intimacy.
Genesis presents marriage as a new, enduring relationship in which a man leaves his parents and holds fast to his wife.
The Hebrew verb translated “cleave” conveys the idea of adhering or holding firmly.
This is not a picture of disposable intimacy.
It is a picture of committed union.
And when Jesus was questioned about marriage in Matthew 19:4–6, He returned to this very passage.
He affirmed that the two become one flesh and taught that what God has joined together, human beings must not separate.
So when Paul quoted Genesis 2:24 in 1 Corinthians 6:16, he was invoking the creation design that Jesus Himself had affirmed.
But notice something important.
Paul did not say that prostitution creates a marriage covenant.
He did not teach that every sexual encounter automatically makes two people husband and wife.
That would go beyond what the passage actually says.

Instead, he applied the language of one-flesh union to show that sexual intercourse creates a real bodily joining, even when it takes place outside the covenant relationship for which God designed it.
This is precisely what makes Paul's warning so serious.
A person can engage in a bodily union without honoring the covenant purpose of that union.
The act does not become meaningless simply because the participants refuse to treat it as sacred.
And that is where Paul's words begin to reach beyond ancient Corinth.
Because our generation has become remarkably skilled at separating physical intimacy from personal responsibility.
We have learned to say things like:
“It didn't mean anything.”
“It was only physical.”
“We weren't serious.”
“It's my body.”
“Nobody got hurt.”
But Paul challenges the assumption underneath those statements.
He insists that what happens through the body matters.
Not because the body is dirty.
Not because sexual desire itself is evil.
Not because God is embarrassed by human sexuality.
But because God created the body with dignity, purpose, and a future.
Sexuality is not a mistake in God's creation.
It is part of His design.
The problem is not that the body possesses sexual capacities.
The problem arises when human beings use God's good gifts in ways that contradict His intentions.
And there is a painful irony here.
Many people search for intimacy because they desperately want to feel loved.
They want to be chosen.
Wanted.
Held.
Seen.
Sometimes they are not even searching primarily for pleasure.
They are searching for reassurance that they matter.
For a moment, another person's attention can feel like an answer to years of loneliness.
For a moment, physical closeness can resemble emotional safety.
But physical intimacy cannot, by itself, guarantee faithful love.
A person may offer access to their body without offering commitment.
Someone may receive affection without receiving honesty.
And a relationship may create intense feelings without possessing the trust, faithfulness, and covenant commitment that make marriage what God intended it to be.
This does not mean every painful sexual experience produces the same emotional consequences.
People are different, and Scripture does not teach that every sexual encounter creates an invisible, permanent mystical bond.
The popular language of unbreakable “soul ties” often goes beyond what 1 Corinthians 6:16 actually establishes.
Paul's point is more precise and more powerful.
Sexual union is real, and its moral significance cannot be erased simply by calling it casual.
But now we must face another question.
Why did Paul choose prostitution as his example?
Because it represented a particularly direct contradiction of the Corinthians' identity in Christ.
In the ancient world, prostitution was a recognizable social reality.
Paul's warning concerned a believer voluntarily joining himself sexually to a prostitute.
He was not declaring that a person involved in prostitution was beyond God's compassion.
He was not assigning equal moral responsibility to people who had been exploited, trafficked, coerced, or abused.
And his words must never be used to shame victims of sexual violence.
Sexual assault is not consensual sexual immorality on the part of the victim.
The guilt belongs to the perpetrator, not the person who was violated.
This distinction matters because the Gospel never gives us permission to place burdens of shame upon people who have already suffered injustice.
Paul was addressing the moral responsibility of believers for their own actions.
And his reasoning was rooted in their relationship with Christ.
Then, in 1 Corinthians 6:17, he wrote something breathtaking.
“But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.” (KJV)
In Greek, the central expression reads:
ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν
ho de kollōmenos tō kyriō hen pneuma estin
“But the one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit.”
The verb kollaō, appearing here in the form kollōmenos, carries the sense of joining or attaching oneself.
It is related to the language Paul had just used to describe joining oneself to a prostitute.
That verbal connection is deliberate.
Paul is contrasting two kinds of union.
In verse 16, he speaks of bodily union through sexual intercourse.
In verse 17, he speaks of spiritual union with the Lord.
He is not suggesting that union with Christ is sexual.
Nor is he claiming that these two relationships are identical.
He is making the Corinthians confront the inconsistency of their behavior.
They belong to Christ.
They are united to Him.
How, then, can they treat their bodies as instruments for conduct that contradicts that relationship?
And suddenly, Paul's warning becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps your struggle is not prostitution.
Perhaps it is pornography.
Perhaps it is adultery.
Perhaps it is a secret relationship you keep justifying.
Perhaps it is a pattern of sexual behavior you have repeatedly promised to abandon.
Perhaps nobody knows.
You still attend church.
You still sing worship songs.
You still share Bible verses.
You still tell people that God is good.
But when the room becomes quiet, there is a battle you are tired of losing.
You know the familiar cycle.
Temptation.
Compromise.
Regret.
Promises.
A few days of determination.
Then the same struggle returns.
And eventually, the most dangerous thought begins to whisper:
“Maybe this is just who I am.”
But listen carefully.
Your repeated failures do not have the authority to redefine what Christ has declared about those who belong to Him.
That does not excuse sin.
It makes repentance possible.
Because the Gospel does not tell us to make peace with the darkness.
It calls us to bring the darkness into the light.
And Paul did not leave the Corinthians without direction.
In verse 18, he gave a command.
“Flee fornication.”
The Greek text begins:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The word pheugete is an imperative from pheugō, meaning to flee or escape.
Paul did not say to entertain temptation until it becomes unbearable.
He did not say to negotiate with it.
He did not tell believers to prove their spiritual strength by remaining as close to sin as possible.
He said to flee.
There is a reason Joseph's response to Potiphar's wife in Genesis 39 remains such a powerful example.
When confronted with sexual temptation, Joseph refused the invitation.
And when she seized his garment, he left it behind and fled.
Sometimes obedience looks less like standing dramatically in front of temptation and more like leaving the room.
Closing the application.
Ending the conversation.
Breaking off the secret arrangement.
Seeking accountability.
Confessing what pride has kept hidden.
Removing access to what repeatedly leads you into sin.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
But because repentance is not merely sorrow over consequences.
It is a turning away from sin toward God.
And if you have been fighting the same hidden battle for years, please hear this.
You do not have to pretend that the struggle is easy.
You do not have to announce your most private failures to strangers on the internet.
But you also do not have to keep protecting a secret that is destroying your peace.
Bring it before the Lord.
Seek the help of a mature, trustworthy Christian.
If the struggle has become compulsive, professional counseling may also be appropriate.
There is no shame in receiving wise help while pursuing holiness.
And remember that temptation itself is not identical to sin.
Jesus was tempted, yet remained without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
The call is not to despair because temptation exists.
The call is to resist it through God's grace.
But Paul's argument still has one more breathtaking revelation.
And it may be the most beautiful part of the entire passage.
After warning believers to flee sexual immorality, Paul asked:
“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?” — 1 Corinthians 6:19 (KJV)
Think about the weight of those words.
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Not because you have lived a flawless life.
Not because you have never struggled.
Not because you have never fallen.
But because God has graciously made His people His dwelling place through the Holy Spirit.
Paul is speaking to believers who had been called out of their former way of life.
In the previous verses, he reminded them of the transformation God had already worked among them.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, he named patterns of unrighteousness that are incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom.
Then he said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (KJV)
Stop there.
“Such were some of you.”
Not because their past had never happened.
Not because their sins were imaginary.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
But because the grace of God had changed their standing before Him and called them into a new life.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Those words are not decorations in a religious speech.
They are declarations of what God had done for sinners through Jesus Christ.
The Corinthians were not a congregation of people who had never known darkness.
Some had lived in serious sin.
Yet the apostle could speak of them as people whom God had washed.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends sin does not matter.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and His mercy is powerful enough to forgive what human beings cannot undo.
Perhaps someone reading this has a past they cannot bear to remember.
A relationship they regret.
A betrayal they wish they could reverse.
Years spent in sexual immorality.
An addiction that stole time, trust, and peace.
Perhaps you have repented, yet still struggle to believe that God could genuinely forgive you.
You can recite the verses.
You know the theology.
But when you look at yourself, all you see is the person you used to be.
And here is what you must understand.
Repentance does not change the historical fact of what happened, but Christ's forgiveness changes the sinner's standing before God.
The cross does not rewrite history by pretending the past never existed.
It rewrites the future by reconciling sinners to God and beginning a work of transformation that sin could never accomplish.
That is why the Gospel is greater than self-improvement.
Self-improvement says, “Become better so you can finally be acceptable.”
The Gospel announces that salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ, and that those who belong to Him are called to walk in the new life He gives.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is the mercy that brings us to Christ and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that connection unmistakable.
And Romans 6 confronts the very idea that grace should become an excuse to continue sinning.
Paul's answer was emphatic.
“God forbid.”
The same grace that forgives also calls us to holiness.
The same Savior who receives repentant sinners commands them to follow Him.
And the same Lord who died for us refuses to treat our bodies as worthless.
Because Paul ends his argument with a declaration that should change the way every Christian understands personal dignity.
“For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.” — 1 Corinthians 6:20 (KJV)
The decisive words are:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
ēgorasthēte gar timēs
“For you were bought with a price.”
The verb ēgorasthēte comes from agorazō, meaning to buy or purchase.
Paul uses the language of purchase to emphasize that believers no longer belong to themselves as autonomous masters.
They belong to the Lord who redeemed them.
Elsewhere, Scripture connects our redemption directly to Christ's sacrificial death.
First Peter 1:18–19 says that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
And Acts 20:28 speaks of God's church as purchased with blood.
The price of redemption was not a financial transaction that human beings could have afforded.
It was the sacrificial death of Jesus Christ.
Consider the contrast.
Sin tells you that your body is available to whatever desire demands.
Shame tells you that your body is ruined beyond restoration.
But the Gospel tells believers that they belong to the crucified and risen Savior.
Your body matters so much that God calls you to glorify Him through it.
And the Christian hope goes even further.
In 1 Corinthians 6:14, Paul reminds the church that God raised the Lord and will also raise believers by His power.
That means the body is not disposable.
It has an eternal future in God's redemptive purpose.
Christian holiness is therefore not hatred of the body.
It is reverence for the God who created it, redeemed His people, and promises resurrection.
And this is why Paul's quotation of Genesis matters so profoundly.
He began with the reality of bodily union.
He moved to the believer's union with Christ.
He commanded believers to flee sexual immorality.
And he concluded by reminding them that their bodies belong to God.
Everything points toward one central truth.
You cannot fully understand Christian sexual holiness until you understand Christian belonging.
We do not pursue purity to make Jesus willing to love us.
We pursue holiness because His grace has called us to belong to Him.
And when we fail, we do not need to invent excuses or surrender to despair.
We confess our sins.
We turn back to Christ.
We trust His mercy.
And we take the next step of obedience.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to manipulate grace.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is hope for the person who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from being loved by God.
And there is a call to repentance for the person who has been using God's patience as permission to continue in deliberate rebellion.
Both need the same Savior.
Both need the same cross.
Both need the same grace.
Perhaps the most tragic thing about sexual sin is not simply that it violates God's design.
It is that people sometimes trade something precious for something that cannot ultimately satisfy.
They exchange truth for secrecy.
Faithfulness for excitement.
Peace for temporary pleasure.
And sometimes they discover too late that what promised freedom has become a form of bondage.
But Jesus Christ is not powerless before the chains we have forged through our own choices.
He came to save sinners.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day.
That is the Gospel Paul preached in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And that is the Gospel at the center of this warning.
Not merely, “Stop sinning.”
But, “You belong to the One who died and rose again. Therefore, live in a way that honors Him.”
What would happen if you began to see your body through that truth?
What would change in your private decisions?
What would happen to the relationship you know is leading you away from obedience?
What would happen to the habits you have been defending?
What would happen if, instead of asking how close you could remain to temptation, you began asking how faithfully you could follow Jesus?
And what would happen if the person drowning in shame finally understood that repentance and forgiveness are not empty religious words?
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you have read this far because there is something in your life you know God has been confronting.
Not through an audible voice.
Not through some mysterious sign.
But through the plain truth of His Word.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you are ready to stop making excuses.
You do not need to make a public spectacle of your repentance.
But you can be honest before God right now.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have treated Your gifts carelessly and allowed desires to lead me away from Your truth. I cannot cleanse my own heart. I need Your forgiveness. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to turn from what dishonors You and to walk in obedience through the power of Your Spirit. Help me remember that my body and my life belong to You. Amen.”
You do not have to explain the details. You do not have to expose your personal history. And you do not have to prove your sincerity to strangers.
But sometimes a simple request for prayer becomes the beginning of an honest conversation with people who will encourage you toward Christ.
Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be living with shame over something they have never told anyone.
Someone may be quietly justifying a relationship that is pulling them away from Christ.
Someone may have stopped attending church because they believe their past makes them unworthy of walking through its doors.
Return to 1 Corinthians 6 when temptation begins to sound reasonable, when shame begins to sound final, or when you need to remember why your body matters to God.
Because this passage is not merely about the danger of sexual immorality.
It is about the dignity of belonging to Christ.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious content that disappears after a few seconds of scrolling.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
But to keep bringing people back to the Scriptures, to repentance, to the cross, and to the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want more people to encounter the Gospel, understand God's Word in its proper context, and discover that following Jesus is not merely a Sunday activity.
It is a life of discipleship.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another meaningful way to participate.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It is not a substitute for repentance, prayer, obedience, or faithful participation in a local church.
And it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe owed to Gospel Warrior.
But it can be a voluntary, prayerful expression of generosity—a recurring gift of support, offered to the Lord as you help make ongoing Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources possible.
In 1 Corinthians 9:14, Paul affirms the principle that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support from that ministry.
In Philippians 4:15–18, he gratefully acknowledges the financial partnership of believers who helped sustain his work.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, he teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion.
That matters.
Because God is not glorified by manipulating people into giving. He is honored by generosity flowing from faith, love, and a willing heart.
It can help sustain the work behind messages like this one and make it possible to reach more readers with biblical truth.
These products are not the Gospel itself, and purchasing them does not make anyone more spiritual.
Those free resources reflect something important about our mission.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And nobody should ever feel that their inability to contribute financially makes them less welcome in this community.
Pray about it.
Give willingly.
Support according to your ability.
And let your generosity be an expression of gratitude to God, not an attempt to earn anything from Him.
A thoughtful share may introduce someone to a biblical truth they have never understood.
A personal invitation may bring a struggling believer into a community where Scripture is taken seriously.
And a simple comment may remind another person that they are not alone in their desire to follow Christ faithfully.
Jesus Christ.
Not an organization.
Not a platform.
Jesus.
He is the One who saves.
He is the One who forgives.
He is the One who calls sinners to repentance.
He is the One who gives new life.
And He is the One to whom every Christian ministry must ultimately point.
So return with me one final time to Paul's question.
Why did he quote, “The two shall become one flesh,” while warning against prostitution?

Because he wanted believers to recognize that sexual intimacy involves a genuine bodily union, that God's design for that union must not be treated casually, and that those who belong to Christ must honor Him with their bodies.
Paul reached back to Genesis because God's original design still mattered.
He spoke of union with Christ because redemption had changed the Corinthians' identity.
He commanded them to flee sexual immorality because grace never makes sin harmless.
And he reminded them that they were bought with a price because the cross gives the believer's life a new purpose.
There is warning here.
Real warning.
But there is also extraordinary hope.
The Corinthians were not told that their past made redemption impossible.
They were reminded that some of them had already been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
And that same Gospel still calls sinners to turn from darkness and come to the Savior.
Perhaps you cannot undo yesterday.
Perhaps there are consequences you must still face.
Perhaps rebuilding trust will take time.
Perhaps obedience will require painful decisions.
But if you come to Christ in repentance and faith, your past does not have to be the final word over your life.
His grace is sufficient to forgive.
His Word is sufficient to guide.
His Spirit is able to strengthen.
And His resurrection is the guarantee that sin and death do not have the final victory.
The most beautiful thing about redemption is not that Jesus pretends your scars never existed, but that He can make a life once marked by sin become a testimony to His grace.
